strengths: Addresses an underexplored and well-motivated problem: existing LLM-based SDG agents focus on deduction/strategy selection but largely ignore the persuasive, listener-directed dimension of communication.

The Stackelberg framing provides an intuitive and reasonably systematic way to operationalize 'persuasion' as a concrete, differentiable training objective (shifting a follower's response distribution), rather than relying on vague notions of eloquence.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span three structurally different SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW), multiple state-of-the-art baselines per game, and consistent improvements are shown when the trained Refiner is combined with each baseline.

Useful ablations, including a reward-decomposition study (positive-only vs. negative-only vs. combined) that yields an interpretable finding (asymmetry between rewarding desired vs. penalizing undesired responses), and a two-stage vs. single-stage / prompt-only refinement ablation that supports the necessity of RL fine-tuning over pure prompting.

Demonstrated generalization of the trained Refiner to unseen backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining, suggesting the learned refinement is not merely overfit to training-time backend styles.
The plug-in design (refining any baseline's utterance) is practically appealing and simplifies integration with prior work.
weaknesses: The core reward signal is questionable: persuasive impact is measured as the log-probability that a frozen open-source Measurer (a copy of the Refiner's own base model) generates an exact pre-specified target utterance, given the candidate utterance. This is a very indirect, high-variance proxy for whether a real follower (often a different, API-based LLM) would actually adopt the desired stance—paraphrased but semantically equivalent responses would receive low reward, and there is no validation (e.g., correlation analysis) showing that this Measurer-based reward tracks actual behavior changes in the real, heterogeneous follower models used at evaluation time.

There is an unaddressed train/test mismatch: during training, the reward computation is given the follower's hidden role rt+1 ('we leverage full information during training'), while at inference this information is unavailable to the leader when identifying intent. The paper does not analyze how much this discrepancy affects the quality/realism of the learned reward or the resulting policy.

No human evaluation of persuasiveness or naturalness of the refined utterances; all evidence of effectiveness is indirect (win rate in self-play among LLM agents), which conflates 'persuasion' with any property that happens to move specific opponent LLMs (e.g., verbosity, assertiveness, or exploiting quirks of particular models) rather than demonstrating genuine, generalizable persuasive skill.

The 'theoretical foundation' (Stackelberg competition, Appendix B) is largely narrative/motivational rather than a rigorous formalization—there is no derivation of an optimal leader strategy, no equilibrium analysis, and no formal connection between the stated mathematical objective (Eq. 13) and the actual GRPO training procedure beyond analogy.

Reproducibility concerns: several baselines and the agent pool depend on closed, versioned commercial APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, GPT-5) without fixed snapshots/dates, which are subject to silent updates and access restrictions, undermining exact replicability of the reported win rates.

Statistical rigor is limited: win-rate differences (e.g., ONUW Ours+ReAct 44.3% vs. ReAct 43.6%) are reported as single point estimates from 500 matches with no confidence intervals or significance testing, making it hard to assess whether some reported gains are meaningful versus noise.

It is unclear whether baseline methods were run under identical conditions/backends as claimed in the original papers or reimplemented by the authors, and whether the 'Ours + Baseline' comparison is entirely fair (e.g., baselines are not also given access to the same refinement infrastructure or an equivalent parameter/compute budget).
The case studies (Appendix E) are hand-picked qualitative anecdotes rather than systematic analysis, and offer limited evidentiary weight for the claimed sophistication of persuasive strategies.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored angle in LLM agents for social deduction games: optimizing utterances specifically for their persuasive effect on the next speaker's response, rather than just role deduction or discrete strategy selection.

The proposed reward (log-probability shift toward desired vs. away from undesired follower responses) is a concrete, differentiable operationalization of 'influence' that can be trained with GRPO without a critic or human preference data.

Very extensive empirical validation: four distinct environments (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW, Sotopia) plus an additional bargaining benchmark (AmazonHistoryPrice), multiple backend LLMs (including held-out GPT-5 and Qwen3-14B for generalization), several ablations (reward-function variants, K sweep, dataset-size sweep, two-stage refinement necessity), and a human-subject evaluation with real Werewolf players.

The 'Ours + Baseline' plug-in design (refining any existing baseline's utterances) is a practical contribution demonstrating that the method is complementary to prior strategy-selection approaches rather than a replacement.

Reasonably detailed prompts, implementation details (LoRA rank, GRPO hyperparameters, compute budget) and case studies are provided, aiding reproducibility and interpretability of what the refiner learns.
weaknesses: The 'Stackelberg competition' framing is mostly rhetorical/intuitive rather than a rigorous game-theoretic formalization; Appendix B offers narrative justification but no formal equilibrium concept, best-response characterization, or proof that the local pairwise optimization approximates a meaningful global solution—so the theoretical contribution is thinner than the framing suggests.

The reward is computed using a fixed proxy 'Measurer' (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) to simulate the follower's response distribution, which differs from the actual (often proprietary) backend LLMs used as opponents at both training and test time; this proxy-follower mismatch is not deeply analyzed and could bias the learned persuasive strategies toward exploiting proxy-model idiosyncrasies rather than genuine persuasion.

Reward computation during training uses privileged information (the next player's true hidden role) that is unavailable at inference, creating a train/test information asymmetry whose impact on policy quality and potential overfitting is not investigated.

No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any win-rate results, despite relatively modest sample sizes (50–500 matches) and some reported gains that are numerically small (e.g., ONUW Ours+ReAct overall 45.1 vs. 43.1); this weakens confidence in the robustness of the claimed improvements.

Evaluation relies substantially on LLM judges (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash) and on backend LLMs from the same families used elsewhere in the pipeline, raising potential self-preference/evaluator bias concerns that are not discussed or controlled for.

Human evaluation is limited to a single game (Werewolf), a small uncompensated volunteer pool (16 students), and does not report inter-rater agreement or demographic/skill controls, limiting generalizability of the human-AI results.

The paper notes but does not experimentally address the observed increase in utterance length during training, an important confound since longer, more elaborate utterances could partly explain persuasive gains independent of the proposed Stackelberg mechanism.
